items.q: A 75-year-old man presents with an acute dissection of the descending thoracic aorta. His blood pressure measures 190/110 mmHg. Justify your plan for his preoperative blood pressure management. (30%) Describe the potential complications of thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) and how you would mitigate them. (70%)
items.model:
> **Evidence:** ESVS 2026 descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal guideline (see source key); ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline (see source key).

> **Examiner emphasis — verified against the [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106410):** Identify descending Type B pathology, justify initial BP/rate control and address TEVAR-specific complications. Do not substitute an emergency Type A/open-rupture answer. Current model/checklist is an educational synthesis, not the College marking scheme.

### Preop

### Blood pressure (30%)

This is a **Type B dissection**. Propagation is driven by **aortic wall stress (dP/dt)** and the BP, so the aim is **anti-impulse therapy**: reduce **heart rate 60–80/min** and **SBP <120 mmHg or the lowest pressure maintaining organ perfusion**, while maintaining organ perfusion.

- **Arterial line** (right radial, as the left subclavian may be involved) and measure both arms.
- **Analgesia** (fentanyl or morphine) as pain drives the BP.
- **Beta-blocker first** (esmolol or labetalol IV) to lower dP/dt and prevent reflex tachycardia; add a **vasodilator** (GTN, nicardipine, or nitroprusside with cyanide caution) only after heart rate control.
- Watch for **malperfusion** (renal, mesenteric, limb, spinal): do not drop the BP so far that organs lose perfusion.

### Intraop

### TEVAR complications and mitigation (70%)

| Complication | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Spinal cord ischaemia** (coverage extent, compromised collaterals, hypotension) | Avoid hypotension, maintain oxygen delivery and collateral supply; assess staging/left subclavian revascularisation. Drain strategy is individualised: 2026 ESVS allows rescue rather than routine prophylactic drainage in extensive TEVAR; have immediate rescue capability |
| **Stroke** (arch manipulation, left subclavian coverage) | Gentle wire work, avoid hypotension, heparin, consider arch vessel protection |
| **Access injury and rupture** (large-bore iliofemoral access) | Imaging of access, cross-matched blood, surgical team ready |
| **Retrograde type A dissection, new tear** | Careful sizing, minimise balloon use, TOE or CT follow-up |
| **Malperfusion, endoleak, graft collapse** | Fenestration or stent, completion angiography |
| **Contrast-associated AKI** | Minimise contrast, hydrate, avoid nephrotoxins |
| **Haemodynamic instability at deployment** | Agree deployment conditions; transient BP reduction, **rapid pacing or adenosine only when required by the device/operator**, with rescue ready; arterial line for beat-to-beat monitoring |
| **Post-implantation syndrome, left arm ischaemia, radiation** | Supportive care, shielding |

**Anaesthesia:** GA is usual (immobility and apnoea), with an arterial line, central access, large-bore IV, heparin (ACT above 250 seconds), blood available, and a critical care bed.

### Postop

Critical-care neurological/limb and organ-perfusion checks, renal function and bleeding surveillance. After exclusion/repair, spinal-perfusion support may require **higher MAP** than the pre-repair anti-impulse target; agree the competing aortic and spinal goals with the team. New weakness requires immediate spinal-cord rescue. Uncomplicated acute Type B dissection starts with medical management; rupture/malperfusion or other complications warrant urgent intervention, while selected high-risk uncomplicated cases may undergo planned subacute TEVAR.
rubric: Identifies Type B dissection and justifies anti-impulse therapy (rate and BP targets)
Uses beta-blocker first then vasodilator, with analgesia
Arterial line, both arms, avoids over-treatment and malperfusion
Lists spinal cord ischaemia and states drain and MAP strategies
Lists stroke, access injury, retrograde dissection, endoleak and malperfusion
Mentions contrast-associated AKI and its prevention
Describes agreed deployment haemodynamics; pacing/adenosine only if required
Covers GA, monitoring, heparin, blood and critical care

items.q: A 75-year-old patient presents for lower limb angioplasty and stenting for peripheral vascular disease. Discuss the challenges in providing anaesthesia for this patient.
items.model:
> **Evidence:** BJA Education: Anaesthesia for lower limb revascularization surgery (2015;15:225–230) (see source key); ASRA antithrombotic regional anaesthesia guideline, fifth edition (2025) (see source key); ESUR Contrast Media Safety Committee Guidelines 2026 (see source key).

> **Examiner emphasis — verified against the [official report](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106434):** Cover comorbidity, local/sedation/regional/GA choices and procedural duration, invasiveness, remote location and limited patient access. Current model/checklist is an educational synthesis, not the College marking scheme.

### Preop

### Patient factors

PVD is a marker of **systemic atherosclerosis**: ischaemic heart disease (often silent), heart failure, **cerebrovascular disease**, hypertension, **diabetes**, **CKD**, **COPD and smoking**, and frailty. Functional capacity is hard to assess because claudication limits exercise. Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel) are continued; statins and beta-blockers continue; diabetic drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors) and anticoagulants need a plan. Rest pain, ulcers and a painful limb may make lying flat difficult.

### Intraop

### Procedural factors

- **Radiology suite** (remote location): limited access to the patient, radiation (lead, distance, shielding), cold room, unfamiliar team and equipment.
- **Duration** is unpredictable (minutes to hours), the patient lies flat and still.
- **Access**: femoral puncture (or brachial or pedal), **heparin** (ACT), contrast load (**contrast-associated AKI**, anaphylaxis).
- **Complications**: arterial perforation or rupture, distal embolisation, haematoma or retroperitoneal bleed, acute thrombosis, and **need for conversion to open surgery**.

### Anaesthetic options

- **Local anaesthetic infiltration with minimal sedation** is often sufficient; this avoids GA in a high-risk patient and allows the patient to report pain.
- **Regional (spinal or epidural)**: effective but sympathetic blockade can cause hypotension; it needs neuraxial safety (timing with antiplatelets and anticoagulants, heparin), and the patient must lie flat.
- **General anaesthesia** if the patient cannot cooperate, the procedure is long or painful, or conversion to open is likely; airway and haemodynamic control, but greater cardiovascular effects.
- **Monitoring** to standard, plus an arterial line in high-risk patients; maintain normothermia; protect pressure areas.

### Postop

### Recovery plan

Recover with limb/access-site and bleeding checks, renal surveillance where indicated, multimodal analgesia and a clear antithrombotic/mobilisation plan. Bed rest is determined by the closure/access protocol, not a universal prolonged requirement.
rubric: Identifies comorbidities: IHD, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes, CKD, COPD
Describes remote location, radiation and limited access
Lists procedural complications and conversion to open surgery
Compares local with sedation, regional and general anaesthesia
Plans monitoring, recovery and groin care
